q: Slow fermentation at deliberately low temperatures, chasing a fruity and floral perfume, is the signature of which approach?
exp: Cool, long fermentation preserves the esters that give melon, pear and banana notes, known collectively as ginjo-ka. The other three names describe starter methods instead.

q: A cloudy white sake still carrying suspended rice solids has been through which treatment?
opts: No dilution, so it is sold as genshu
A coarse filtration, so it is sold as nigori
No charcoal filtration, so it is sold as muroka
Cedar cask ageing, so it is sold as taruzake
exp: Nigori is filtered through a wide mesh that lets rice solids through, so the bottle is usually rolled gently before pouring. Muroka is a different claim altogether: charcoal filtration was skipped, which keeps colour and texture but leaves nothing in suspension.

q: Bottles marked nama have to be kept refrigerated from brewery to glass. What has been left out?
exp: Most sake is pasteurised twice, once before storage and once at bottling. Skipping it leaves live enzymes and a fresher, livelier flavour that spoils if it warms up.

q: Which term tells you that no water was added to bring the strength down before bottling?
exp: Genshu usually lands between 17 and 20 percent instead of the customary 15 or 16. It suits ice or a splash of water at the table.

q: Deliberately matured sake that has darkened to amber and turned nutty and savoury goes by which name?
exp: Koshu is a small niche because the overwhelming majority of sake is meant to be drunk young, ideally within a year of leaving the brewery.

q: Which vessel would you set on the table to pour from rather than to drink from?
exp: The tokkuri is the narrow-necked flask. The ochoko is the small cup, the masu the square cedar box, and the sakazuki the flat ceremonial dish.

q: A delicate daiginjo is going to the table. How should it reach the guest?
opts: Poured over a full glass of ice
Warmed gently in a flask of hot water
exp: Heat drives off the fine esters that the brewer worked at low temperature to build. Sturdier junmai and honjozo take warming far better.

q: Warming sake to roughly 50 degrees Celsius before service is described by which word?
exp: Atsukan is the hot end of the scale and nurukan a gentler 40 or so. Reishu means chilled and hiya means served at ambient temperature without heating.

q: Most sake reaches the guest at what alcoholic strength?
exp: The mash itself ferments to nearly 20 percent and is then cut with water before bottling. Undiluted genshu skips that step and stays higher.

q: An opened bottle is going back into the refrigerator. What should the guest be told about it?
opts: It can sit out at room temperature indefinitely
It oxidises quickly once it is opened
It will keep improving for several months
It should be frozen to preserve it
exp: Sake has no tannin and little acidity to defend it once air gets in, so an open bottle is best finished within a few days. Treat it the way you would treat an open white wine, or more carefully still.

q: Separating alcohol from water inside a still relies on which difference between the two?
exp: Ethanol boils near 78 degrees Celsius and water at 100, so the vapour coming off is richer in alcohol. Distillation concentrates alcohol; it never creates any.

q: A still is charged, run off, emptied and then charged again for the next run. Which type behaves that way?
exp: Batch working leaves more congeners in the spirit, which is why pot stills suit flavour-driven categories. A column still and the small alambic armagnacais both run without pause, and a worm tub is a condenser rather than a still at all.

q: The distiller sets aside the first and last portions of a run and keeps only the middle. What are those two outer fractions called?
exp: Heads carry volatile, solvent-like compounds and tails carry heavy, oily ones, so only the middle cut, the hearts, goes forward from this run. They are not waste: most distillers hold them back and put them into the next charge, which is why a still house wastes very little.

q: A cask quietly loses a few percent of its contents to the air every year in the warehouse. What is that loss called?
exp: Liquid evaporates through the staves, and in a humid warehouse the strength falls while a dry one loses more water. The devil's cut is the spirit soaked into the wood itself.

q: A bottle sold in the United States reads 80 proof. What strength is in the glass?
exp: American proof is simply twice the alcohol by volume. Eighty proof is the legal floor for most spirit categories sold there.

q: Which white grape supplies the overwhelming majority of the base wine for Cognac?
exp: The base wine is thin, sharp and low in alcohol, which is unappealing to drink and ideal to distil. Folle Blanche and Colombard are also permitted but planted far less.
